periods.analysis: Harborview’s Population Growth Rate opened this reporting arc at 2.2%, with no prior quarter in this series for comparison, and it is comfortably green against the >=1.5% target. The Planning counter logged steady intake from the East Harbor multifamily permits, the Bayline infill cottages, and move-ins tied to the Seaview Tech Park hiring cohort. From a council-facing standpoint, this is the kind of growth we want to show: strong enough to confirm demand, but still measurable through our quarterly reporting cycle and parcel-level data checks. Finance and Community Development are aligned on the count, which matters because clean population data drives transportation, parks, and utility assumptions downstream.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green result by keeping the Growth Dashboard reconciliation on the first-Friday close, using permit finals, utility activations, and school enrollment snapshots as the three check sources. Extend the practice by adding the East Harbor and Bayline project IDs to the Q4 annex so departments can see which neighborhoods are carrying the growth. Please keep the council packet language simple: Harborview is growing at 2.2%, and the administration is tracking the service impacts in real time.

periods.analysis: Population Growth Rate remained green at 1.9%, down 0.3 percentage points from 2.2% in 2024-Q3, which is a normal late-year easing rather than a signal of softness. Move-ins slowed after the summer lease cycle, while several Harbor Landing units shifted certificate-of-occupancy timing into January. The important point for council is that even with the quarter-over-quarter dip, Harborview is still above the >=1.5% target and continuing to attract households. Staff also completed a helpful address-file cleanup with the Assessor’s Office, so the Q4 figure is not only green, it is better documented.
periods.recommendations: Sustain performance by keeping the Planning, Utility Billing, and GIS address match in the monthly closeout checklist, especially for new apartment deliveries. Extend the green result by preparing a Q1 move-in watch list for Harbor Landing Buildings B and C, the North Pier townhomes, and the Bayline cottages that slipped past year-end. For the council update, note the 1.9% result and the -0.3 movement plainly, then emphasize that the rate remains above target and operationally understood.

periods.analysis: Population Growth Rate moved back up to 2.1%, an increase of 0.2 percentage points from 1.9% in 2024-Q4, keeping Harborview solidly green. The rebound matches what we saw operationally: January and February utility starts picked up in the Harbor Landing buildings, and the Welcome Desk cohort from the Seaview Tech Park relocation program converted into local addresses. This is a good example of why the quarterly cadence matters; Q4’s timing issue resolved into Q1 activity rather than disappearing demand. Data quality also improved because GIS tagged 312 new residential address points before the reporting lock, reducing the manual follow-up burden for departments.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green trend by continuing the pre-lock data huddle five business days before quarter close, with Community Development, Utility Billing, GIS, and Finance all signing off. Extend the work by adding a short “new resident pressure points” note for Parks, Library, and Transit so service teams can plan around the 2.1% growth rate. Please keep nudging permit applicants to submit unit-phasing schedules early; that is the easiest way to make Q2 reporting clean and council-ready.

periods.analysis: Population Growth Rate rose again to 2.3%, up 0.2 percentage points from 2.1% in 2025-Q1, and remains green with meaningful room above the >=1.5% target. The increase lines up with spring completions along the Coastal Connector corridor, including the Mariner Row townhome phase and the first occupancy block at Harbor Landing C. From a strategy perspective, this confirms that Harborview’s housing pipeline is translating into actual resident growth, not just permitted inventory. Departments are handling the reporting rhythm well, and the shared dashboard is making it easier to connect growth to traffic counts, recreation registration, and library-card starts.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the 2.3% green result by keeping the Coastal Connector occupancy tracker active through the summer move-in season. Extend the practice by asking Transportation and Parks to add one growth-response action each to their Q3 updates, such as signal timing checks on Route 14 and added evening field slots at Pelican Park. For council, frame this as healthy, managed growth supported by timely reporting and interdepartmental coordination.

periods.analysis: Population Growth Rate held green at 2.2%, down 0.1 percentage points from 2.3% in 2025-Q2, which is essentially a stable summer plateau. Seasonal turnover was higher near the waterfront rental blocks, but it was offset by owner-occupied closings in Mariner Row Phase 2 and continued hiring at Seaview Tech Park. The slight -0.1 movement is worth naming, but it does not change the story: Harborview remains a high-demand coastal suburb growing above target. I also appreciate that departments met the reporting deadline without a second reminder this quarter, which makes the council narrative cleaner and more credible.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green result by keeping the summer turnover review in place for waterfront census tracts HV-03 and HV-04, where lease timing can blur the quarter-to-quarter picture. Extend the analysis by pairing the 2.2% population figure with school enrollment and Route 14 ridership in the next dashboard refresh, so growth impacts are visible without overloading the council packet. Continue the one-week pre-deadline reminder to departments; it is light-touch, but it is working.

periods.analysis: Population Growth Rate remained green at 1.9%, down 0.3 percentage points from 2.2% in 2025-Q3, repeating the expected year-end cooling pattern we saw last winter. Several multifamily lease-ups slowed during the holiday window, and the final unit batch for the North Pier townhomes moved into early 2026 occupancy records. Even with the -0.3 shift, Harborview is still above the >=1.5% target, which is the key council takeaway. The stronger administrative story is that staff can now explain the movement by project timing, not guesswork, because the permit, address, and utility datasets are lining up more consistently.
periods.recommendations: Sustain performance by preserving the year-end reconciliation routine and documenting any occupancy deferrals by project name before the Q4 close is finalized. Extend the green result into 2026 by creating a January move-in bridge list for North Pier, Harbor Landing remaining units, and the Bayline accessory dwelling permits. In the council memo, show the 1.9% value, the -0.3 movement, and one sentence on seasonal timing so the dip is transparent but not overstated.

periods.analysis: Population Growth Rate increased to 2.1%, up 0.2 percentage points from 1.9% in 2025-Q4, returning to the same spring rebound pattern as the prior year. The January bridge list did its job: North Pier closings, delayed Harbor Landing leases, and Bayline ADU activations all appeared in the utility-start file before the reporting lock. This keeps Harborview green and reinforces the message that our growth is resilient, trackable, and supported by actual residential occupancy. The dashboard evidence is now strong enough that departments can use it for planning rather than just after-the-fact reporting.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green result by making the January bridge list a standing Q1 tool, with project owners assigned before the holiday close each year. Extend the work by asking Finance to use the 2.1% growth rate in the midyear revenue and service-demand assumptions, while noting the +0.2 quarter-over-quarter movement. Please keep the department deadline at five business days before packet production; the cleaner inputs are helping everyone look prepared.

periods.analysis: Population Growth Rate reached 2.3%, up 0.2 percentage points from 2.1% in 2026-Q1, matching the strongest point in this eight-quarter arc and staying green. Spring activity was broad-based, with Coastal Connector move-ins, Mariner Row final certificates, and new employer-sponsored relocations from the Seaview Tech Park expansion all contributing. The two-year pattern is now clear: Harborview cools modestly at year-end, rebounds in Q1, and accelerates in Q2 while remaining above the >=1.5% target throughout. That is a strong council story for a financially healthy, AA-rated city, provided we keep tying population growth to service planning rather than treating it as a standalone win.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the 2.3% green result by continuing the cross-check among permits, utility activations, GIS address points, and school enrollment before every quarterly lock. Extend the program by publishing a concise Growth-to-Services appendix for Q3 that links this population trend to park capacity, arterial travel times, library demand, and water-utility planning. Assign Community Development to maintain the project-level pipeline list, because the next council question will be where the growth is landing and how prepared we are.

periods.analysis: Growth is 1.31%, down from 1.34% in June but above the 1.2% target.
periods.recommendations: Continue checking occupied addresses against permits and utility activations before the Council update.
